faq.a: No, there is no curative treatment; management is supportive.
Human‑to‑human transmission is extremely rare and only via contaminated instruments.

exam: A 45‑year‑old presents with progressive ataxia and memory loss over 3 years. What is the most likely diagnosis? — GSS; look for cerebellar atrophy on MRI and PRNP mutation.
A patient with suspected prion disease has a negative 14‑3‑3 CSF test. What next? — Proceed to PRNP sequencing and repeat CSF testing; 14‑3‑3 is not specific.
Why is sodium hydroxide used for prion decontamination? — It denatures prions, overcoming their resistance to standard sterilisation.
What distinguishes GSS from sporadic CJD on MRI? — GSS shows cerebellar atrophy; sporadic CJD shows cortical ribboning.
Which drug should be avoided in a patient with GSS and renal impairment? — NSAIDs; use paracetamol instead.
A family member of a GSS patient wants genetic counselling. What is the key point? — Autosomal dominant inheritance; 50 % risk to offspring; offer PRNP testing.
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: A rare inherited prion disease presenting with progressive cerebellar ataxia and dementia. Diagnosis relies on clinical features, neuroimaging, EEG and CSF prion protein testing. No curative therapy; supportive care is mainstay.

sections.p: GSS is a familial prion disorder caused by pathogenic mutations in the PRNP gene. It follows an autosomal dominant pattern with variable penetrance and age of onset.
The infectious agent is a misfolded prion protein (PrP^Sc) that induces conformational change in normal prion protein (PrP^C).

t.b: Confirm presence of misfolded prion protein in CSF or brain tissue; a positive result supports diagnosis when clinical picture fits

sections.p: Human-to-human transmission is extremely rare, occurring mainly via contaminated surgical instruments or organ transplantation. Inheritance is the predominant route.

t.b: Assess risk of instrument contamination; if exposed, use 1 M NaOH + 20 % hydrogen peroxide for 1 h

b: Ataxia onset 20–30 yrs after symptom onset
sections.p: GSS manifests as progressive cerebellar ataxia, dysarthria, and later dementia. Early signs may mimic other neurodegenerative disorders.

t.b: MMSE <24 indicates dementia; track decline over 6‑month intervals

sections.p: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by neuroimaging, EEG, CSF biomarkers and genetic testing.

t.b: Look for cerebellar atrophy and T2 hyperintensity in cerebellar peduncles; absence of cortical lesions helps exclude Creutzfeldt‑Jakob disease
Periodic sharp wave complexes may appear but are non‑specific
Positive supports prion disease but not specific to GSS
Identify pathogenic mutation; confirms diagnosis and informs family counselling

sections.p: No disease‑modifying therapy exists. Management focuses on symptom control and multidisciplinary support.

t.b: Use only if seizures occur; avoid valproate in patients with hepatic dysfunction common in low‑resource settings
Use NSAIDs cautiously due to renal impairment risk

b: Rapid progression and cortical ribboning on MRI → sporadic CJD
sections.p: Remember GSS is a prion disease with autosomal dominant inheritance and late‑onset cerebellar ataxia. Genetic testing is definitive. Distinguish from sporadic CJD by age of onset and imaging patterns.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid neurological decline, new seizures, or severe cognitive impairment
